claims.text: Conventionally cast titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloys typically have coarse grains.
Conventionally cast titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloys typically exhibit elemental segregation.
Conventionally cast titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloys typically have an inhomogeneous phase distribution.
Rapid SPS heating and short dwell times limit grain growth.
Rapid SPS heating and short dwell times minimize phase segregation.
Processing pre-alloyed powder by SPS produces a finer-grained microstructure than conventional casting of the same alloy.
SPS produces a more uniform distribution of alloying elements than conventional casting of the same alloy.
SPS suppresses coarse precipitates relative to conventional casting of the same alloy.
The finer, more homogeneous SPS microstructure hinders grain-boundary sliding at elevated temperature.
Hindering grain-boundary sliding improves high-temperature creep resistance.
The refined SPS microstructure improves high-temperature yield strength.
The SPS-processed alloy will have higher elevated-temperature yield strength than the same conventionally cast alloy.
The SPS-processed alloy will have better elevated-temperature creep resistance than the same conventionally cast alloy.
SPS is anticipated to improve key elevated-temperature mechanical metrics by approximately 10–20%.
The predicted mechanical benefit applies over approximately 800–1200 °C.
Maintaining compositional homogeneity and phase stability is necessary for the intervention to be effective.
Processing parameters outside an appropriate sintering-temperature and dwell-time range may eliminate the predicted benefit.
Alloy compositions outside the defined high-entropy range may not exhibit the predicted benefit.
